summary: Automatic host fencing slice 4b: the watchdog engine, arming, the durable armed report and the watchdog exclusion proof — plus the five findings of slice 4a's independent review. The engine is the Debian sbd daemon in diskless watchdog-only mode; Nex Core writes /etc/default/sbd and enables sbd.service and never opens the watchdog device itself, so one device has one owner. A nested three-host QEMU lab settled the properties and corrected two of this plan's own assumptions. FIRST: diskless sbd has no quorum source without Pacemaker (its only inputs are a shared block device and -P), so with SBD_PACEMAKER=no it starts, holds the watchdog open and NEVER expires it — a host that reads as armed and could never be fenced. The configuration is therefore SBD_PACEMAKER=yes and a host whose pacemaker.service is not running is not armed and says so. SECOND: no-quorum-policy=freeze and a bounded self-reset are mutually exclusive. Measured with freeze, a partitioned host was still running after two minutes; measured with suicide, the same host left the quorate partition 8.6 s after its cluster link went down and had reset and rebooted by 15.7 s while the two survivors stayed quorate and did not reset. So the plan's freeze must become suicide, clustered storage's current freeze has to change with it when the pool owns the CIB, and until then ArmLocalWatchdog READS the policy and refuses to arm a cluster that would keep an inquorate host running rather than report a protection that does not exist. THIRD: Debian's sbd.service is RefuseManualStart and exists only as a dependency of corosync.service, so a host whose cluster is already running can only begin feeding its watchdog at that cluster's next start — Nex Core enables sbd, changes nothing else and reports arming as pending with maintenance mode as the way out, and NEVER restarts a running cluster to arm a watchdog. Disarming is systemctl disable plus SIGTERM, which makes sbd close the device with the kernel's magic character; measured in the lab, three armed hosts released the device and none reset. Where the kernel was built with nowayout that close does not stop the timer, so Nex Core refuses to try and reports that the host stays armed until it is rebooted. PoolMember.watchdog_armed is the host's own durable, replicated report carrying the device class, the timeout and the pool membership generation it armed at; its staleness rule is that generation and not a clock, because the host that must read it is a promotion candidate whose master has gone. The watchdog proof kind implements the plan's rule change exactly: the target's armed report at this generation, a quorate Corosync partition of more than one host that excludes the target read from corosync-quorumtool and never from Nex's own heartbeats, and a continuous monotonic hold of at least twice the target's timeout and never less than a minute, with the target reappearing, quorum being lost, an observation gap or an agent restart each restarting the clock from zero. Refusal before the bound says how long remains. Two-host pools never produce one. Emulated watchdogs are a new kind: i6300esb, ib700wdt and wdat_wdt are real chips and also what a hypervisor shows a guest, so a host whose DMI vendor is a hypervisor reports 'emulated' — armed like hardware so a nested lab exercises the path, labelled everywhere so no proof resting on one reads as hardware evidence. INDEPENDENT REVIEW OF THIS SLICE found four defects in the half of the engine no current install can reach, each of which becomes live the moment a pool cluster exists, and all four are fixed here with regression tests that fail on revert. FIRST, the armed report and the proof checked two different generation counters: arming stamped the membership generation while the promotion path passed the authority generation, which diverges immediately, so a pool would have shown 'Watchdog . armed' and then refused to promote. The generation is now read off the member record itself, where PoolMembership.Valid pins it equal to the membership's, and is never a parameter a caller could get wrong; a new test drives poolPromotionFenceReadiness and fencePoolExcludedHosts rather than the proof function directly, which is what let it through. SECOND, a failed re-verification only wrote a sentence into a field nothing reads, so a host whose cluster had since been given no-quorum-policy=freeze by a clustered-storage repository kept reporting armed and a proof would have been granted against a host measured still running after two minutes; 'armed' now means armed and still verified, and a host whose re-verification fails withdraws its own report stripped of every field a proof could rest on. THIRD, the continuity clock tolerated an observation gap three times longer than the shortest bound, so a target could leave, rejoin and leave again unseen; the gap is now derived from the bound itself (a quarter of it), Corosync's ring identifier restarts the clock on any membership event no sampling could catch, and the quorum reading moved onto its own tick instead of riding a worker that can spend minutes talking to a management controller. FOURTH, the disarm happened before it was recorded, so a master that died mid-way left a replica saying armed about a host that had stopped feeding its watchdog; the record now goes first in both directions and a host that cannot record a withdrawal stays armed and says so. Two further measurements were taken in a rebuilt lab: Debian's sbd package leaves sbd.service ENABLED on install, and the unit is RequiredBy=corosync.service, so an unmanaged sbd would be pulled into the next cluster start of an existing clustered-storage host with the distribution's configuration instead of Nex Core's - nex-core-local's postinst now disables it unconditionally and the reconcile keeps it disabled on every host the pool has not asked to arm; and disarming was measured against a live cluster, where systemctl disable is inert while a SIGTERM leaves the unit failed on that Requires edge, so a disarm now disables only and reports 'disarm pending' until the next cluster stop, mirroring the arming rule. stonith-watchdog-timeout is settled at 30s rather than the lab's initial 10s, which was shorter than the measured 15.7 s reset. Slice 4a's review findings F1-F11 are closed in the same change: WritePoolFenceCredential now parses replicated credential bytes before writing a mode-0700 file that a fence agent and Pacemaker run as root; Core refuses a fence password whose leading or trailing whitespace fence_ipmilan would strip; the plan and guide now say the restarted-master restriction follows fence exposure and not the Host fencing switch; the checklist gives host IDs in a new hosts field so the page prints display names; the fence-device prerequisite is computed from the fence-device method so a watchdog cannot satisfy its own prerequisite; the never-opens test now forbids exec and open as well as the path spelling; PoolHostWatchdog.identity and .devices are deleted because nothing read them; a one-host pool is no longer told it is fenced through its management controllers; and ExecutePoolHostFencing gained the Valid() and second mastership check its siblings have. sbd is added to installer/packages.txt and the nex-core-local Depends with its licensing review. API impact: changed contract, implemented both sides. LEFT OPEN AND MATERIAL: Nex Core does not form a pool's Corosync/Pacemaker cluster and writes none of its properties, so in practice nothing arms by itself anywhere yet; and no physical watchdog of any model has been read, armed or expired.

guide.reason: Arming is behaviour an operator must meet before it can reset a host, so docs/guide/pool-authority-and-recovery.md's 'Host fencing, and the watchdog line' is rewritten: that Nex Core arms these watchdogs itself and an armed host that loses quorum resets itself; a table of every line a row can now show, including 'Watchdog · armed' as the row's own badge, 'Watchdog · armed (emulated)' and what an emulated device is and is not evidence of, a host with no Pacemaker cluster, a cluster whose policy would keep an inquorate host running, arming pending with maintenance mode as the way out, a device another program already holds, an armed report from an earlier record of the pool, and a host that could not be disarmed because its kernel was built with nowayout; the checklist's four lines with the quorum line now real; that turning the setting off disarms cleanly at the next reconcile pass and what nowayout means for that; and a new paragraph on promoting over a host that reset itself — that nobody powers it off, that Nex Core refuses until the bound has passed and says how long remains, and that the clock restarts on any flap including the surviving host's own agent restarting. A 'Limits you should know about in this release' block states plainly that no physical watchdog has been tested, that Nex Core does not yet form a pool's cluster or write its properties so nothing arms by itself yet, and that a host whose cluster is already running arms at its next cluster start. The automatic-provisioning section gains the paragraph slice 4a's review asked for: that letting Nex Core configure a management controller is what opts a pool into the restarted-master restriction, that the Host fencing switch does not govern it, and where to read the consequence. The page's status list is corrected. docs/guide/README.md needs no change: the page is listed and its title is unchanged.

api.reason: No new route. PoolMember gains watchdog_armed (PoolWatchdogArmed{armed, kind, device, timeout_seconds, fencing_generation, detail, observed_at}), durable in the master's replicated membership and carried on the existing peer route POST /api/v1/pool/advertise as a fifth key beside origin, system_uuid, bmc and watchdog: recorded in the calling member's own row only, refused with 400 when an armed report names a kind that could not reset a machine independently of its kernel or a string is over length, and written only when it changes so a settled pool does not re-sign its authority. Its staleness rule is fencing_generation (the pool membership generation the host armed at) and not a clock, because a promotion candidate reads it out of the signed replica after the master is gone; observed_at is when the finding last changed, as PoolHostBMC.observed_at is, and nothing decides from it. PoolHostWatchdog.kind gains 'emulated' and LOSES identity and devices, which nothing read. PoolFencePrerequisite gains hosts ([]string): Core ends detail before naming hosts and puts their IDs there, because only a client knows display names. StorageClusterFenceStatus gains method ('watchdog', absent meaning the fence-device proof every older Core produces) and watchdog (PoolWatchdogExclusion{kind, timeout_seconds, armed_generation, held_seconds, bound_seconds, partition}). PoolPromotionFenceVerified now takes the whole PoolMember instead of its fence profile, and dispatches: a watchdog proof is re-checked against the target's durable armed report, the generation, the recorded bound and a partition that excludes the target and has more than one host in it. PoolFenceMethod kind 'watchdog' can now be 'ready'. PoolPromotionHost.fence_kind names 'watchdog' where that is the method, and the old-master-exclusion check's sentence carries the remaining wait per host. protocol.PoolQuorum was deliberately NOT put on the wire: it is one host's live reading and lives in vmhost beside the code that takes it. Version compatibility both ways: a Core too old to report watchdog_armed leaves it absent, which is never readiness and never a proof; a Core too old to accept the field ignores it and the member keeps reporting; an older master reports no prerequisite hosts and the client shows the sentence as written; method is absent on every proof an older Core made, which is exactly the fence-device meaning, so no stored proof changes meaning across an upgrade. The Controller relays watchdog_armed in poolMemberFence and stores nothing. docs/api/{openapi,local-openapi,peer-openapi}.json and the generated reference are updated; python3 scripts/generate_api.py --check passes and tests/test_api_contract.py passes (74 tests).

roadmap.reason: The published roadmap describes shipped capability at a coarser grain than one fencing slice. The plan records what 4b settled and what it left open, and the two open items — Nex Core forming a pool's Corosync/Pacemaker cluster and writing its properties, and physical-hardware evidence — are named as acceptance gates that are still open.

state.reason: Whether a host has armed its watchdog is that host's own report about its own machine, recorded by the pool master in the membership record it owns and replicated with the rest of the pool's records. The decision that governs it is the pool's Host fencing setting, which was already master-owned. The watchdog exclusion proof is made by a surviving Core out of the durable record it holds and the pool's own Corosync quorum, and is recorded in that host's own durable transfer record exactly as a fence-device proof is. Nex Controller relays the setting, displays the master's reports and keeps nothing: no armed state, no quorum reading, no continuity clock and no proof.
state.record: Durable, on the pool master, in pool-peer.json: PoolMember.watchdog_armed (each host's own armed report, with the pool membership generation it armed at, written only when it changes), beside the PoolMember.watchdog capability and PoolMembership.host_fencing_disabled that slice 4a added. It rides the existing signed authority replica to every member, which is what lets a promotion candidate read it after the master is gone — that is the whole reason it is durable rather than an observation. Durable on the proving host, in its own transfer record: the StorageClusterFenceStatus of a watchdog exclusion, with its PoolWatchdogExclusion evidence, bound to pool, host, operation and generation like every other proof. NOT durable, deliberately: this host's Corosync quorum reading and the monotonic continuity clock behind condition (c), which live only in the agent's memory — a restarted agent starts every clock from zero, which is the honest answer to 'how long has this held' when nothing was watching, and is asserted by a test. Also not durable: the fence readiness overlay and the prerequisite checklist, unchanged from slice 4a. On the host itself, Core-owned and not pool state: /etc/default/sbd and the enabled state of sbd.service, both of which Nex Core re-derives from the pool's records on every reconcile pass. A fresh Controller recovers every one of the durable items from inventory.managed.membership reported by the master; there is no Controller table, cache or file for any of it.

verification.method: Go unit tests against fakes for sbd, systemd, corosync-quorumtool and the watchdog sysfs tree, in-process multi-host pool labs over the real mutual-TLS peer transport, React unit tests and a real-browser review of the new states, plus a disposable nested three-host QEMU lab for the physical engine properties the tests cannot reach. RESULTS, all run in this working tree on 2026-09-22: go build ./... PASS; go vet ./internal/... PASS; gofmt clean on every file touched; go test -count=1 ./internal/... PASS (all packages); go test -race -count=1 ./internal/agent/ ./internal/vmhost/ PASS; npx tsc --noEmit PASS; every web/src/*.test.mjs PASS; python3 scripts/generate_api.py --check PASS; python3 -m unittest discover -s tests PASS; python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -p 'test_repository_privacy.py' PASS; python3 scripts/check_docs.py --worktree PASS. NESTED LAB (the QA evidence page docs/qa/2026-09-22-automatic-host-fencing.md, three Debian QEMU guests on a private VDE switch, each with an emulated i6300esb, running corosync, pacemaker and sbd with exactly the configuration renderSBDConfig writes): detection read from the real guests matches Nex Core's classification — sys_vendor QEMU, no driver link, identity 'i6300ESB timer', timeout 30, nowayout 0, state inactive, which classifies as hardware by identity and then as emulated by vendor. ARMING RESET NOBODY: all three hosts came up with corosync, sbd and pacemaker active and the watchdog device held, and no boot_id changed. AN UNRELATED SERVICE RESTART ON AN ARMED HOST RESET NOBODY. PARTITION WITH no-quorum-policy=freeze: the partitioned host left the quorate partition and was STILL RUNNING after two minutes — the measurement that corrected this plan's assumption. PARTITION WITH no-quorum-policy=suicide (the QA evidence page docs/qa/2026-09-22-automatic-host-fencing.md): the same host left the quorate partition at 8.6 s and had reset and rebooted by 15.7 s, the two survivors stayed quorate and neither reset. CLEAN DISARM (the QA evidence page docs/qa/2026-09-22-automatic-host-fencing.md): three hosts measured armed (sbd active, watchdog active), then systemctl disable plus SIGTERM released the device on all three (watchdog inactive) and NONE reset. Pacemaker reported have-watchdog=true and accepted stonith-watchdog-timeout=10s. GO TESTS: the three conditions and every refusal in TestAWatchdogProofNeedsAllThreeConditions (before the bound, with the refusal naming the wait; after the bound as real evidence; and another operation, another host, another generation, a claimed bound shorter than the rule, a partition containing the target and a partition of one host all refused); TestAWatchdogProofIsRefusedForATargetThatCouldNotHaveReset (never armed, reported disarmed, software watchdog, armed at an earlier generation); TestEveryFlapRestartsTheContinuityClock (a held partition proves; the target reappearing destroys it; it does not immediately return when the target leaves again; losing quorum destroys it; and an agent restart destroys it); TestATwoHostPoolNeverProducesAWatchdogProof. ARMING STATE MACHINE: TestArmingFollowsTheSettingAndIsRecordedOnceAtTheCurrentGeneration (armed at the pool's generation, twenty further passes move neither the membership generation nor the authority digest and perform no further arm or disarm, and turning the setting off disarms every host cleanly); TestNoWayOutIsReportedRatherThanResettingTheHost; TestFallingToTwoHostsDisarms; TestAHostIsNeverArmedAgainstItsOwnMachine (a device another program holds, and an sbd that will not start, are each reported and the unarmed report carries no evidence a proof could rest on); TestAWatchdogIsReadyOnlyWhenArmedAtThisGenerationInsideAQuorum (including that an armed watchdog does NOT satisfy the fence-device prerequisite); TestAnArmedReportFromAnEarlierGenerationIsNotReadiness. ENGINE: TestSBDIsConfiguredForDisklessWatchdogOnlyMode; TestArmingAnAlreadyArmedHostRestartsNothing; TestArmingAHostWhoseClusterIsAlreadyRunningIsPendingAndRestartsNothing; TestAHostWithNoClusterIsNotArmed; TestAClusterThatKeepsAnInquorateHostRunningIsNotArmed; TestDisarmingIsCleanAndRefusesNoWayOut; TestLocalQuorumReadsCorosync, including a regression for the quorum-device column the lab exposed, where reading the third field would have made every host's name 'NR'. DETECTION: TestAWatchdogOnAVirtualHostIsEmulated over three hypervisor vendors and a physical one; the strengthened TestWatchdogDetectionNeverOpensTheDeviceNode now refuses os.Open, os.Create, os.WriteFile, exec.Command and wdctl in the detection source as well as the path spelling. BROWSER REVIEW: the real pool-members and pool-promotion modules bundled with the project's own esbuild into the QA evidence page docs/qa/2026-09-22-automatic-host-fencing.md (never web/dist) and driven in headless Chromium through Playwright over five fixture reports — armed with a confirmed controller, armed by watchdog alone, armed on an emulated device, the no-cluster and arming-pending states, a device another program holds, a checklist that names hosts, the nowayout disarm failure, and a two-host pool. Captures were inspected: an armed host carries 'Watchdog · armed' as its own badge with Core's consequence sentence under it, an emulated one reads 'Watchdog · armed (emulated)', a host whose controller is confirmed keeps the BMC badge and gets the watchdog on its own line without duplication, and the checklist prints core-c and core-d rather than host-c and host-d. No console error was raised and the keyboard toggle opens no dialog. ONE DEFECT WAS FOUND AND FIXED, then re-captured: the pool's summary line still read 'Every host in this pool can be shut out by another', which is untrue of a host protected by its own watchdog; it now reads 'by another host, or by its own watchdog'. REVIEW FIXES, each verified by reverting it in a source-only scratch copy under the QA evidence page docs/qa/2026-09-22-automatic-host-fencing.md and confirming the regression fails: finding 1 by TestTheWatchdogProofAndReadinessAgreeThroughTheRealPromotionPath, which drives the preflight's poolPromotionFenceReadiness and then fencePoolExcludedHosts on a pool whose two generation counters have been made to diverge, and which reported 'readiness says the master can be shut out by its watchdog, the promotion path says recorded=false usable=false' on the reverted code; finding 2 by TestAnArmedReportIsWithdrawnWhenReverificationFails, which reported 'a host whose re-verification failed still reports armed'; finding 3 by TestAnUnobservedFlapRestartsTheContinuityClock, which reported 'an observation gap of 3m0s is not shorter than the minimum bound 1m0s' and separately asserts a Corosync ring change restarts the clock; finding 4 by TestAHostIsNeverDisarmedBeforeThePoolRecordsIt, which reported 'a member disarmed while the pool's record still said it was armed'; F1 by TestOnlyProducerFormatFenceCredentialBytesAreWritten, which reported 'bytes that are not what Nex Core writes were accepted into an executable file' for all four payloads; and F2 by TestAFencePasswordAFenceAgentWouldAlterIsRefused and TestAPaddedFenceAccountPasswordIsRefusedAtTheBoundary, which both reported 'a password a fence agent would alter was accepted'. SECOND LAB RUN (an untracked local lab directory, rebuilt; VMs since torn down): the Debian unit presets captured immediately after apt-get install and before anything disabled them read sbd=enabled, corosync=enabled, pacemaker=enabled - so the package does enable sbd on install. Disarm against a live armed cluster (the QA evidence page docs/qa/2026-09-22-automatic-host-fencing.md): after systemctl disable on all three hosts, corosync, sbd and pacemaker were all still active and every watchdog still held, i.e. disabling is inert; after systemctl kill -s TERM on one host, that host released the device (watchdog inactive) and did NOT reset (boot id unchanged), corosync and pacemaker stayed active and the node stayed quorate, but the unit ended 'failed' - Debian's ExecStop runs /bin/kill -TERM $MAINPID with an empty MAINPID, which the journal shows as kill's usage message. No clustered filesystem was mounted for that measurement, which is why Nex Core takes the conservative branch and never signals the daemon.
untested: NO PHYSICAL WATCHDOG DEVICE OF ANY MODEL HAS BEEN READ, ARMED OR EXPIRED, AND NO PHYSICAL HOST HAS BEEN RESET. Every timing in this record was measured in nested QEMU guests with an emulated i6300esb, which is a device the hypervisor resets and not evidence about a chipset TCO, an AMD SP5100, an HP iLO timer or an IPMI watchdog. The plan's acceptance gate requiring physical-hardware evidence that names the exact models tested is OPEN. SBD_WATCHDOG_TIMEOUT=5 is sbd's own default and a judgement, not a measurement against real hardware whose driver may round or refuse it.

NEX CORE DOES NOT FORM A POOL'S COROSYNC/PACEMAKER CLUSTER AND WRITES NONE OF ITS PROPERTIES. Arming happens only where a cluster is already running and its no-quorum-policy is already suicide. No cluster Nex Core configures today says suicide - clustered storage writes freeze - so in practice NOTHING ARMS BY ITSELF ANYWHERE in this slice. That is safe and honest, because an unarmed host is never reported as protected and the row says why, but it is not the feature the plan describes. It also means the arming success path, the arming-pending path, the disarm path and the whole proof are unreachable in any current install: they are covered by tests and by the nested lab, not by a running deployment. The remaining work is a slice of its own and is scoped in the plan.

stonith-watchdog-timeout=30s AND PoolWatchdogBound's 60 s FLOOR REST ON ONE NESTED-LAB RUN of each policy, on a two-second polling loop: the true reset happened somewhere between 8.6 s and 15.7 s. Both numbers are deliberately several times the measured worst case, but the distribution has not been characterised, nothing was measured under load, and a loaded physical host may take longer for Corosync to declare lost. Nex Core does not write stonith-watchdog-timeout at all yet; the number is recorded for the slice that will.

NO CLUSTERED-STORAGE POOL HAS BEEN RUN WITH SBD ARMED, and no GFS2 filesystem or DLM was mounted in any measurement. The interaction the plan cares about - that DLM recovery on the quorate side waits out stonith-watchdog-timeout before treating a node with no other fence device as fenced - is upstream behaviour that was reasoned about and not exercised. Changing clustered storage's no-quorum-policy from freeze to suicide is a change to a running clustered filesystem's safety behaviour and must be proved with a filesystem mounted, with I/O in flight, before it ships. The disarm measurement against a live cluster has the same gap, which is why Nex Core never signals the daemon.

THE ARMING-PENDING AND DISARM-PENDING PATHS ARE TESTED AGAINST A FAKE SYSTEMD. That Debian's sbd.service is RefuseManualStart, and that the package leaves it enabled, were both read from the installed unit and the live guests; that a host in maintenance mode then arms cleanly as its cluster restarts, and releases the device as its cluster stops, has not been exercised end to end, because Nex Core does not start or stop the cluster yet.

THE NOWAYOUT BRANCH IS NOT MEASURED. Every lab guest reported nowayout=0, so the claim that the timer does not stop when the device is closed on such a kernel rests on the kernel's documented behaviour, not on an observation. Its effect here is only on the sentence an operator is shown; the pool's record says not armed either way.

THE POSTINST'S sbd DISABLE IS NOT EXERCISED BY A PACKAGE INSTALL TEST. tests/test_core_local_package.py passes and the line follows the same deb-systemd-helper pattern as the cluster units beside it, but no host was upgraded from a build without sbd in Depends to one with it, which is the case the line exists for.

NO WHOLE CONTROLLER WAS REBUILT AGAINST A LIVE LAB POOL. Controller replacement is proved at the level this slice owns: the armed report is in the master's durable replicated membership, the Controller mirrors it and stores nothing, and the Go tests assert both.

THE BROWSER REVIEW USED MOCKED API DATA IN A FIXTURE PAGE, not a running Controller against real hosts. It proves the wording, the badges, the checklist names and that no state is hidden; it does not prove the projection end to end, which the Go and Controller tests cover separately.

F2's WHITESPACE REFUSAL IS A STRUCTURAL FIX, NOT A MEASUREMENT. That fence_ipmilan strips the whitespace around what its password script prints was reported by slice 4a's reviewer and could not be executed here, because fence-agents is not installed on this workstation. Core now refuses such a password at record time, which removes the divergence whichever way the agent behaves; no fence agent was run to confirm the strip.

ALL OF SLICES 1-3's OUTSTANDING ITEMS REMAIN: no physical management controller has been contacted, no host has been powered off, no RMCP+ session has been authenticated by a Core-created account, and the Redfish Host Interface (SMBIOS type 42) is still not built.
